records.document: Constitution and By Laws of the Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas, adopted June 16, 1971, as revised and annotated incorporating Amendments I through XXIII, published July 2023
records.locator: Art. XIII (Tribal Court System), Secs. 1, 3(c), 5-7
records.quote: The Peacemakers are vested with authority to mediate disputes pursuant to operations and procedures established by Tribal Council ordinance.
records.findings: Art. XIII Sec. 1 vests the court system in a Tribal Court, Court of Appeals and a Peacemaker Court. Sec. 3(c) calls the Peacemaker Court a venue of limited jurisdiction whose mission is to resolve disputes toward a mutual agreement promoting healing through tribal customs, and gives Peacemakers authority to mediate under procedures set by Tribal Council ordinance. Secs. 5-7 cover appointment (Council, four-year terms), qualifications and removal. The constitution does not say how a case reaches the Peacemaker Court or whether agreements are enforced; that is left to ordinance. Record title, citation and kind are supported; only the stale note ('not reviewed') is wrong. Lead session: cited to the July 2023 publication, the version in effect, after checking that Art. XIII, Secs. 1, 3(c) and 5-7 read the same there (Art. XIII unchanged since Amendment XXI, Nov. 13, 2015).

first_reading.quote: The Peacemakers are vested with authority to mediate disputes pursuant to
first_reading.findings: Article XIII establishes a Peacemaker Court as one of the tribal court venues, a venue of limited jurisdiction to resolve disputes by mutual agreement, with Peacemakers authorized to mediate (Sec. 3(c)). The record's title, citation (Constitution and By-Laws) and kind (peacemaking) are supported. The stored note says the constitution was not reviewed for peacemaking content, which is no longer true.

records.document: Bishop Paiute Tribal Workers' Compensation Ordinance for the Paiute Palace Casino; footer 'Work Comp Ordinance 2.18.16'
records.locator: Section 9 (A to M), printed pp. 5-8
records.quote: Any Employee or Dependent who disagrees with a decision made by the Administrator may file a written request for a hearing before the Appeals Board.
records.findings: Section 9 is titled DISPUTE RESOLUTION and has A Administrative Review (employee may request review within thirty (30) days of final written determination; administrator responds within 60 days), B hearing before Appeals Board (request within 30 days of the administrator's written decision; hearing within 90 days), C three-member board, L 'All Decisions of the Board are final', M benefits approved in the original written decision continue during the action. One overstatement: only an Employee (not a Dependent) is given the right to request administrative review in 9.A; Employee or Dependent may request the Appeals Board hearing in 9.B. Also the hearing may be requested without a written decision if the Administrator fails to decide within 90 days. Numbers (30 days, three members) read correctly; no OCR errors found.

records.document: Blue Lake Rancheria, Blue Lake Housing Authority Dispute Resolution Ordinance, Ordinance No. 04-02, adopted by the Business Council April 2, 2004 (5 for, 0 against)
records.locator: Sections 1-9; 5(A)-(B) waiver limits and 360-day notice (p. 1-2); 6(B) arbitration (pp. 2-5); 7 no waiver of Tribe's immunity (p. 5)
records.quote: BLHA shall have the power to consent, on behalf of BLHA only, to being sued in courts or to have claims against it resolved through arbitration; provided, however, any such waiver shall be memorialized in the form of a resolution adopted by the governing body of BLHA.
records.findings: Text supports every claim: consent only by governing-body resolution (5.A); waiver limited to damages enforcement, injunctive relief/specific performance, and an action to compel arbitration (5.A.1.a-c); written notice within 360 days after claim accrues (5.B.1); agreements to arbitrate valid, irrevocable and enforceable (6.B.2); Tribal Court order confirming award, not subject to review or modification (6.B.6.c); no further appeal (6.B.7); Section 7.A preserves the Tribe's own immunity. Nuances: the 360-day notice is in Section 5.B, not 6, and Tribal Court roles apply only 'if and after it is established' (otherwise BLHA may consent to California Superior Court). No OCR errors found.

records.document: Tribal-State Compact between the State of California and the Cher-Ae Heights Indian Community of the Trinidad Rancheria, with Interior Department letter dated Jan. 21, 2026 (deemed approved)
records.quote: Disputes that are not otherwise resolved by the process described in subdivisions (a) through (c), above, or other mutually agreed means, may be resolved in the United States District Court
records.findings: Checked every step in the record: written notice, written response within 15 days, meet and confer within 30 days (Governor or designee with Tribe's CEO or gaming agency director), then federal district court or, if no federal jurisdiction, state court; sec. 13.3 limits relief to injunctive, specific-performance and declaratory (no damages or restitution, except money the compact expressly requires), with mutual limited sovereign-immunity waivers; sec. 13.2 preserves mediation by mutual agreement. Record omits sec. 13.4: after exhausting 13.1(a)-(c) and a 30-day notice to cure, either party may sue in federal court for a declaration of material breach, with 60 days to cure, and the court may then order enforcement or termination of the compact. First reader's addition of 13.4 is right.

first_reading.quote: Disputes that are not otherwise resolved by the process described in subdivisions (a) through (c), above, or other mutually agreed means, may be resolved in the United States District Court
first_reading.findings: Sec. 13.1(a)-(c) requires written notice, a written response within 15 days and a meet-and-confer within 30 days, and 13.1(d) allows court resolution in federal or state court. Sec. 13.3 limits the waiver to injunctive, specific-performance and declaratory relief, and 13.2 allows mediation by mutual agreement, all as the record says. The summary omits Sec. 13.4, which allows a separate federal-court action for a declaration of material breach after a 30-day cure notice, and that can lead to termination, so 'relief only' is overstated. The record's approved date (2026-01-26) is not printed in the text; the Interior letter is dated Jan. 21, 2026.

proposed_changes.summary: The parties exchange written notice and a written response within 15 days and must meet and confer within 30 days; disputes still unresolved may be taken to the United States District Court (or a state court if federal jurisdiction is lacking) for injunctive, declaratory or specific-performance relief only (no monetary damages), under a limited waiver of sovereign immunity; a separate federal-court action for a declaration of material breach, after a 30-day notice to cure, may lead to termination of the compact (sec. 13.4); mediation or other methods may be used by mutual agreement.

records.document: Siletz Tribal Court Rules and Procedures, Siletz Tribal Code Sec. 3.001 et seq., Sec. 3.017 amended 4-17-15 (Res. 2015-118)
records.locator: Siletz Tribal Code Part II (Court Personnel), Secs. 3.010, 3.017; also Secs. 3.004(b), 3.005(b), 3.008(b)
records.quote: The assigned mediator shall meet with the parties in the case and shall attempt to reach an agreed resolution to the case.
records.findings: Text read. Sec. 3.010: the Chief Judge sets up a panel of mediators who are not Associate Judges and work under the Chief Judge or an Associate Judge. Sec. 3.017: Chief Judge appoints the panel for the District Court and Community Law Court; mediators are assigned to cases by the Chief Judge of the branch; the mediator meets the parties and tries for an agreed resolution, which must be written and approved by the Chief Judge or a delegated Associate Judge (approval not unreasonably withheld). Related provisions the record title does not mention: Sec. 3.004(b) requires a mandatory mediation program for Community Law Court disputes, Sec. 3.005(b) a District Court mediation program that may require mediation of some categories, and the commercial court section requires mediation within 30 days in contract disputes. First reading's proposal is accurate; I add the mandatory-mediation cross-references.

records.document: Siletz Community Law Court, Siletz Tribal Code Sec. 3.300, Ordinance 3.300 (adopted 9/21/01, Res. 2001-296), amended by Resolution 2005-361, Sept. 16, 2005
records.locator: Siletz Tribal Code Secs. 3.300-3.333 (Chapters 1-7)
records.quote: Mediate disputes among persons involved in the peacemaking process by attempting to get them to agree as to the nature of the problems affecting them
records.findings: Text read in full. Sec. 3.300 aims to give formal support and enforcement to traditional mediation. Case entry: a written request to the Tribal Court (Sec. 3.308) or transfer of a pending civil or criminal case, which needs the written consent of all parties and which any party can block by objection (Secs. 3.309, 3.325-3.326); the Chief Judge grants or denies, the Community Law Court Judge appoints Gwe-shvt-naga/Peacemakers from a Tribal Council roll with party consent (Secs. 3.303, 3.311-3.312). Peacemakers mediate, use traditional ways, may lecture on tribal teachings, may compel participants to meet and may request subpoenas; they cannot decide a dispute unless all parties agree in writing (Secs. 3.304-3.305). Agreements may be converted into a Community Law Court judgment, enforceable like any Tribal Court judgment and not appealable (Secs. 3.317-3.320). The record's NARF note is accurate but the first reading's summary left out entry, enforcement and binding effect, which I add. Case types: family strife, extended family, neighbor disputes, alcohol, small business matters of $2,500 or less (Sec. 3.302).

first_reading.quote: Mediate disputes among persons involved in the peacemaking process by attempting to get them to agree as to the nature of the problems affecting them
first_reading.findings: The text supports the kind (peacemaking): the Community Law Court and Gwe-shvt-naga/Peacemakers mediate disputes, may use traditional ways and instruct on tribal teachings (Sec. 3.304(b)), may obtain subpoenas (Sec. 3.315), and civil matters are referred only with all parties' written stipulation (Sec. 3.326). The record's citation 'Sec. 3.300' is only the purpose section, and the ordinance runs to Sec. 3.333, so the title and locator are too narrow. The NARF description is accurate but incomplete. The stored verification (read-in-full) now has a basis.

records.document: Colville Tribal Code Chapter 5-2 Juveniles (September 2010 version), Secs. 5-2-191 to 5-2-197 amended 12/16/04 (Res. 2004-799) and 2/17/05 (Res. 2005-108)
records.quote: The probation officer shall refer all cases in which a minor is involved under this Chapter to the Colville Tribal Peacemaking Circle.
records.findings: Read the scanned pages (8-9). 5-2-191: after the custody hearing the probation officer investigates within 3 days and either recommends no action or refers the matter to the Peacemaking Circle. 5-2-192: the probation officer shall refer all cases involving a minor under the chapter to the Circle, with notice of date, time and place to the minor, parent and counsel. 5-2-193: nothing said or received in the Circle is admissible in an adjudicatory hearing or other proceeding against the minor. 5-2-194: peacemakers may refer to a community agency, order supervision terms, accept voluntary restitution, ask the Court to enforce agreements, recommend that the prosecutor file a petition, or order any other remedy including traditional remedies. 5-2-195: probation officer reviews progress every 30 days and may ask the Circle to reconvene. 5-2-197: the Juvenile Court must refer to the Circle on receipt of a petition if it has not yet been tried, and may continue the hearing on the Circle's recommendation. Referral is mandatory ('shall'). The chapter also contains minor-in-need-of-care procedures, and 5-2-192 says 'all cases ... under this Chapter', but the referral steps are written along the juvenile-offender track, so coverage of need-of-care cases is by the general wording only. The record's description, based on NARF, left out these specifics.

first_reading.quote: The probation officer shall refer all cases in which a minor is involved under this Chapter to the Colville Tribal Peacemaking Circle.
first_reading.findings: Sec. 5-2-192(a) requires referral of all cases involving a minor under the chapter to the Peacemaking Circle, which covers juvenile offender and child-in-need-of-care cases; Sec. 5-2-197 requires the court to refer to a Circle upon petition if none has been held. Sec. 5-2-192(b) requires notice; Sec. 5-2-193 bars use of Circle statements in adjudication (the nearest provision to 'confidentiality'); Sec. 5-2-194(d) lets the Circle ask the Court to enforce agreements. The record's summary and mandatory-referral claim are supported. The stored note says the code text was not read, which is no longer true.

apply.description: Under the Colville juvenile code the probation officer must refer all cases involving a minor under Chapter 5-2 to the Colville Tribal Peacemaking Circle, with notice of the date, time and place to the minor, parent or guardian and counsel; the Juvenile Court must also refer a case on receiving a petition if it has not already gone to the Circle. At the Circle the peacemakers may refer the family to a community agency, order supervision terms, accept voluntary restitution, ask the Court to enforce any agreement, recommend a petition, or order any other remedy including a traditional one. Statements made in the Circle cannot be used as evidence against the minor, and the probation officer reviews progress every 30 days and may have the Circle reconvene.

records.document: Statutes of the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation, Family Law Code, as amended through Resolution No. 24-017 (March 4, 2024)
records.locator: Family Law Code Ch. 4, Sec. 4.03(A)-(F) (PDF pp. 8-9 of 95)
records.quote: In any proceeding under the Family Law Code, the matter may be set for mediation of the contested issues before or concurrent with the setting of the matter for hearing.
records.findings: Text read. 4.03(A): court may set contested issues for mediation, and may mandate it on its own motion, rule or custom at any time. (B) purpose: reduce acrimony, resolve property, parenting-contact and child-support issues; mediator makes best efforts to settle. (C) court alone keeps the list of qualified mediators, may order costs paid by one or both parties, and may pick a mediator if parties cannot agree. (D) mediator reports any agreement to the court and counsel. (E) if no resolution after 90 days the court may decide the remaining issues. (F) a party who objects files a show-cause petition and the court orders mediation or lets the case proceed; mediation is waived on a finding of likely severe emotional distress, and a domestic-violence act within 10 years can support a per se finding. The record (title only, NILL link) has no summary; first reading's summary is accurate and I add the reporting step and domestic violence detail. The proposed link is in the project's capture index for this document.

records.locator: Workers Benefit Code ch. 9, secs. 9.01-9.03 (pp. 18-19)
records.quote: the claimant’s attorney’s fees will be approved with a maximum limit of 10% of the total benefit award, or $5,000, whichever is less.
records.findings: Read the tribe's own PDF in full for ch. 9. Sec. 9.03 exists with the heading in the record, but it sits in the Workers Benefit Code (workers' compensation), not a general arbitration code. 9.01 sets the process: a claimant appeals an Administrator decision by written contested claim within 30 days; the Tribal Employment Benefits Committee (TEBC) appoints an arbitrator; the arbitrator's decision is final and binding except for appeal to the Umatilla Tribal Court within 30 days (reviewed on a deferential standard). 9.03(A): if the arbitrator awards more than the Administrator's original determination, claimant attorney fees are capped at 10% of the award or $5,000, whichever is less, paid over and above benefits; fee disputes are filed with the arbitrator under TEBC rules. 9.03(B): each side bears its own physician/expert costs, not reimbursable whatever the outcome. Record had no summary; the NILL table-of-contents locator and 2014 date are superseded. Agrees with the web reading.

records.document: Fort McDowell Yavapai Nation Tribal Gaming Ordinance (Law and Order Code Ch. 21), amendments adopted by Res. 2020-018 on Feb. 4, 2020; NIGC approval letter dated May 11, 2020
records.locator: Gaming Ordinance (Law & Order Code Ch. 21), Chapter 8 Patron Dispute Resolution, subsections (a)-(g) (ordinance p. 21-22)
records.quote: If a patron files a written complaint with the TRA alleging that the Gaming Facility Operator has failed to pay winnings owed to the patron
records.findings: Text read. (a) If operator and patron cannot resolve a dispute over winnings or losses, operator tells patron of right to complain to the Tribal Regulatory Agency (TRA) and, if $500 or more, notifies the TRA at once. (b) operator files written position within 15 days; TRA investigates and decides validity and relief. (c) TRA mails decision within 30 days. (d) effective on receipt. (e) aggrieved party may petition for review within 30 days; Commission decides within 60 days, hearing or on the record. (f) patron with a dispute of $500 or more may file in Tribal Court within 60 days; the Tribal Court's disposition is final and binding, and it upholds the TRA/Commission unless arbitrary, procedurally defective or unsupported by substantial evidence. (g) tort claims by patrons go only to Tribal Court under the Tribal Tort Claims Act. First reading's summary stops at the Commission and omits the Tribal Court review (f) that makes the outcome final and binding, and the tort-claim route (g). Not a settlement forum for losses: it is an administrative complaint and appeal path.

first_reading.locator: Gaming Ordinance (as amended by Res. 2020-018), Chapter 8, subsections (a)-(e)
first_reading.quote: (b) Complaint. If a patron files a written complaint with the TRA alleging that the Gaming Facility Operator has failed to pay winnings owed to the patron
first_reading.findings: The title and subject match: Chapter 8 governs patron disputes over winnings. The 2020 text, though, sets a $500 notice threshold to the TRA, a 15-day report by the operator, a TRA decision within 30 days, and a petition for review decided by the Gaming Commission within 60 days. The record's citation does not name the 2020 amendment, and it has no summary; the record's as_of (2018-12) predates the 2020 text.

apply.citation: Fort McDowell Yavapai Nation Gaming Ordinance (Law and Order Code Ch. 21, as amended by Res. 2020-018, adopted Feb. 4, 2020), Chapter 8, Patron Dispute Resolution
apply.summary: Patron disputes over gaming winnings or losses: if the operator and patron cannot resolve it, the operator tells the patron of the right to complain to the Tribal Regulatory Agency (TRA) and, for $500 or more, notifies the TRA. The operator files a written position within 15 days, the TRA investigates and issues a written decision within 30 days, and either party may petition for review by the Gaming Commission, which decides within 60 days. A patron with a dispute of $500 or more may then file in Tribal Court within 60 days, which reviews for arbitrary action, procedural error or lack of substantial evidence, and its decision is final and binding. Patron tort claims go only to Tribal Court under the Tribal Tort Claims Act.

proposed_changes.summary: Authorizes a roster of Peacemakers, tribal members at least 50 years old who are known and respected in the community, appointed by the Tribal Council with the Chief Judge and Culture Committee, to mediate disputes between parties before or during a Tribal Court case, only with the consent of all parties. Peacemakers hold informal conferences, make sure all relevant facts and views are heard, and encourage agreement. A request is filed with the Court Clerk, the Judge refers the case within ten days unless a party objects, and a party may object to the Peacemaker appointed. Anyone convicted of a crime in the last five years may not serve.

apply.citation: Hopland Band of Pomo Indians Tribal Code, Title 12, Chapter 12-1 Tribal Court Ordinance, Sections 12-1.20.020 and 12-1.100
apply.summary: The Tribal Council, advised by the Chief Judge and Culture Committee, keeps a roster of Peacemakers (tribal members at least 50 years old, known and respected, with no conviction in the past five years) to mediate disputes in an optional, non-adversarial process that needs every party's consent and can be used before any lawsuit is filed. A party files a request with the Court Clerk; if no one objects the Judge refers it to a Peacemaker within ten days, and any party may object to the Peacemaker or decline once the rules are explained. Lawyers may not represent parties. A settlement is written and signed by the parties and the Peacemaker and is an enforceable agreement, treated as the final judgment if a lawsuit is pending; discussions are confidential, and parties may still go to Tribal Court if peacemaking fails.

first_reading.locator: Sections 33.01.02(O) and 33.01.16(A)-(F), Title 33 Youth Code
first_reading.quote: No substantive information obtained at the conference may be admitted into evidence at a court hearing or any other court proceeding unless such information can be substantiated by outside evidence.

The stored kind is not contradicted.

records.quote: When a petition is filed with the Clerk of the Court, the Peacemaker Mediation Forum shall be used prior to proceeding to a formal Court hearing.

first_reading.locator: Chapter 3.05 Tribal Court, Sections 3.05.010(E) and 3.05.100(A)(1)-(3)
first_reading.quote: When a petition is filed with the Clerk of the Court, the Peacemaker Mediation Forum shall be used prior to proceeding to a formal Court hearing.
first_reading.findings: Every claim matches. The Peacemaker Mediation Forum is part of the Tribal Court and hears disputes between parties before trial (3.05.100(A)(1)); its use is required after a petition is filed, before a formal hearing; it is a nonadversarial method for disputes between tribal members and others within the Tribe's jurisdiction, with guidelines reflecting traditions and modern methods (A(2)); and parties may continue in court if mediation fails (A(3)). The legal basis (3.05.100, Res. 10-R-111 section 10.9) matches. The text does not limit case types, so the record's civil and other is a reasonable reading.

records.quote: The District Court of the Kiowa Tribe is hereby authorized to utilize peacemakers, which shall be a division of the District Court of the Kiowa Tribe
records.findings: Read pages 10-16 images. S.2: District Court authorized to use peacemakers as a court division under Kiowa customs; court assigns and supervises. S.3 qualifications. S.4: peacemaker has jurisdiction over a referred matter if all parties agree to be bound by the peacemaker's decision; otherwise case goes back to court. S.5: peacemaker cannot force resolution or adjudicate what parties cannot resolve voluntarily. S.6 judge appoints. S.8-10: parties file written request, or motion for referral; court grants a joint motion, may decline for delay or unsuitability, may refer on its own motion only if all consent. S.11: no procedural/evidence codes apply, attorneys only at peacemaker's discretion; agreement written and signed by all parties, with proposed dismissal order; court reviews and, if sufficient, endorses and files it as a final, non-appealable order; no agreement after 60 days or on certification, matter returns to court; S.13 orders enforceable like other District Court orders; S.14 statements inadmissible as settlement negotiations. Record's relationship_to_court and enforcement are blank and note is stale.

first_reading.locator: Court Codes, Kiowa Tribe Peacemaking Act (PDF pp. 10-16; Act pp. 1-7): Sections 2-16 read; Sections 1 (title), 17 and 18 not read
first_reading.quote: The District Court of the Kiowa Tribe is hereby authorized to utilize peacemakers, which shall be a division of the District Court of the Kiowa Tribe and which shall operate in accordance with the customs and traditions of the Kiowa people.
first_reading.findings: The record's description holds. Section 2 authorizes the District Court to use peacemakers as a division of the court, operating under Kiowa customs (2A-B). Section 6 has the judge appoint a peacemaker where parties agree to traditional methods; Sections 8-10 provide for written requests, motions and joint motions to refer, and a court-initiated referral only when all parties consent. Sections 11-12 cover the agreement and proposed order filed as a final, non-appealable order, and Section 13 makes orders enforceable like other District Court orders. Section 4 lets peacemakers decide a referred matter if all parties agree to be bound, which the record's summary does not mention; Section 5 bars forcing a resolution. The approval resolution and date are not in the record. The note's statement that details came from the table of contents is out of date.

record_before.name: Peacemakers of the District Court (Kiowa Tribe Peacemaking Act)
record_before.description: The Act authorizes the District Court of the Kiowa Tribe to use peacemakers and provides for use of Kiowa Tribe traditions and customs, referral of existing actions, agreements and proposed orders, and enforcement of orders.
record_before.legal_basis: Kiowa Tribe Peacemaking Act, Sections 1-18
record_before.note: Details from the Act's table of contents and opening section as quoted by NCORJ; the structure parallels the Choctaw Nation and Chickasaw Nation acts.

apply.description: The Act authorizes the District Court of the Kiowa Tribe to use peacemakers, as a court division operating under Kiowa customs and traditions, to resolve disputes in a fair, informal and inexpensive way. Parties may request peacemaking in writing or move to refer a pending case, and the court may refer on its own motion only if all parties consent. A peacemaker cannot force a resolution; a peacemaker may decide a referred matter only if all parties agree to be bound.
apply.relationship_to_court: Peacemaking is a division of the District Court, which assigns, supervises and certifies peacemakers. The court refers cases by order on a party's request or motion (it must grant a joint motion) or on its own motion with all parties' consent; unresolved matters go back to the court.
apply.enforcement: The parties' signed written agreement and proposed order are reviewed by the District Court and, if sufficient, entered as a final, non-appealable order, enforceable like any other order of the District Court (Section 13). Statements made in peacemaking are not admissible in court proceedings.

apply.locator: Guidelines Sections 1-12 (printed pp. 2-9); Sections 13-15 and appended forms not read
apply.summary: The Tribal Court's Peacemaking program (Odenaang Enjinoojimoying) works alongside the court system for minors and adults. Cases may come from the Tribal Court, other tribal or state courts, agencies or a person's own request, in juvenile status and non-status matters and adult civil disputes; a request may be made by offering tobacco or another medicine, or by court order or personal request, and Peacemakers may deny a case in writing. Sessions are voluntary, led by two Peacemakers (one man, one woman) who direct the process but not the content, and are confidential except for child-abuse reporting. The signed agreement is a legally binding contract, and the Tribal Court enforces it by court order if participants do not follow it. Peacemakers must be at least 21, volunteers, and tribal members or tribal employees, and are certified after training.

records.document: Waganakising Odawak Tribal Code of Law (WOTCL), Title XVIII Post Constitution Resolutions, version 2024.2, codified through March 1, 2024; Sec. 18.278 source Tribal Resolution #121015-06
records.locator: WOTCL Title XVIII, Ch. 2, Sec. 18.278 (recitals A-D, resolution paragraphs 4-5)
records.quote: The authorizations and statements contained in Tribal Resolution 020214-01 regarding all provisions in the February 7, 2014 Financing Documents
records.findings: Read the full section. It authorizes swap documents with Wells Fargo to hedge interest rates on an existing loan (Tribal Resolution 020214-01), not a new loan. Paragraph 4 reaffirms the Dispute Resolution Provisions of the 2014 Financing Documents (governing law, forum selection, arbitration, limited waiver of sovereign immunity, waiver of exhaustion of tribal remedies, use of tribal forums) and applies them to the swaps, except that New York law and consent to New York state and federal (Manhattan) courts apply to the swap documents. Paragraph 5: Tribal Court gives full faith and credit to federal or state court awards and tribal police may execute tribal court judgments. The arbitration law itself (Exhibit A) is in Sec. 18.507. The first reader's summary is right on the loan point but omits the New York forum and enforcement terms.

first_reading.locator: WOTCL Title XVIII, Ch. 2, Sec. 18.278 (title, recitals A-D, resolution paragraph 4)
first_reading.quote: AFFIRMING ADOPTION OF LAW GOVERNING THE ARBITRATION OF DISPUTES RELATED TO THE LOAN (INCLUDING THE SWAP)
first_reading.findings: The statute title confirms the arbitration point, but the record's summary is wrong on the main transaction. Sec. 18.278 authorizes swap documents and appropriations for swap payments with Wells Fargo, related to a loan already authorized by Tribal Resolution 020214-01 (Feb. 7, 2014); it does not authorize a bank loan. It affirms (not newly adopts) the arbitration law for the loan. The operative paragraph reaffirms the Dispute Resolution Provisions, including arbitration, for the swap documents.

proposed_changes.summary: Authorizes swap documents and appropriations for swap payments with Wells Fargo Bank, related to an existing loan (Tribal Resolution 020214-01); affirms adoption of the law governing arbitration of disputes related to the loan, including the swap; and addresses security interests.

records.locator: WOTCL Title XVIII, Ch. 4, Sec. 18.400(7.20)(a) (recitals F-H, resolution paragraphs 4-8, Exhibit A)
records.quote: The Tribal Council hereby enacts as a law of the Tribe the “Limited Arbitration Provisions” set forth in EXHIBIT A attached hereto.
records.findings: Read in full including Exhibit A. Approves a PNC Bank loan (initial $26.5 million: Term Notes of $13 million and $13.5 million) to refinance an existing note and fund casino projects, and approves the loan documents' dispute resolution provisions and limited waivers of sovereign immunity as binding and independently enforceable tribal law. Exhibit A sections 3-8: agreements to arbitrate valid and enforceable; a party may apply within one year to a Tribal Court to confirm an award; the court does not review or modify the award but may decline to enforce on four listed grounds (fraud, partiality, misconduct, excess of powers); confirmed award docketed and enforced like a civil judgment; no appeal; police support. The first reader's summary is accurate but omitted how the awards are enforced.

records.quote: waives sovereign immunity to the benefit of Dropbox and no other party for the limited and sole purpose of consenting to arbitration, with any arbitration judgment enforceable in accordance with California law
records.findings: Read in full. Recital B: Accounting needs to exchange confidential documents with citizens; recital C: the Executive tried to revise Dropbox's Business Agreement (an adhesion contract) to provide for arbitration enforceable only in Tribal Court but Dropbox refused. Resolution D: limited waiver for the sole purpose of consenting to arbitration, judgment enforceable under California law, limited to the value of the contract. The record's note wrongly says it concerns a loan or contract authorization; it is a vendor agreement and the summary should state the enforcement and cap. Agree with first reader.

first_reading.quote: waives sovereign immunity to the benefit of Dropbox and no other party for the limited and sole purpose of consenting to arbitration, with any arbitration judgment enforceable in accordance with California law, provided, that this waiver is limited to the value of the contract.
first_reading.findings: The summary is supported: a limited waiver of sovereign immunity for arbitration with Dropbox. The record's note, however, says the statute authorizes 'a loan or contract', and the text shows a vendor Business Agreement (an adhesion contract) for confidential document exchange, not a loan. The arbitration judgment is enforceable under California law and the waiver is limited to the contract's value; the record does not say so.

records.document: Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe, Chapter 3: Operation of Peacemaker Court (no enactment date printed); Peacemakers Court brochure (no date printed)
records.locator: Brochure pp.1-2; Chapter 3 Secs. 1, 2(a)-(f), 3(b)(1), 4
records.quote: Final binding decision is agreed upon by all parties
records.findings: Brochure supports ideal cases, no lawyers, voluntary participation, one male and one female peacemaker, binding decision agreed by all parties, and the bilingual principles; no date printed. The 'Chief Judge of the Supreme Court' supervision claim is not in either text: Chapter 3 Sec. 3(b)(1) says certified peacemakers must agree to serve under the direction and supervision of the Chief Judge, and the Judiciary Committee certifies them and Tribal Council appoints them. Chapter 3 adds how a case gets there (written request to the Court Clerk before filing, or a party's request to the District Court judge after filing; the other side may decline and a non-response counts as agreeing in the pre-filing route; the Chief Judge then appoints two peacemakers), excludes criminal matters, says the court cannot compel participation, and Sec. 2(f) says an agreement is a final decision without appeal. The texts do not say how the agreement is enforced.

The record's claim that the Peacemakers Court is supervised by the 'Chief Judge of the Supreme Court' is not in any text read: Chapter 3 Section 3(b)(1) says certified peacemakers serve under the direction and supervision of the Chief Judge, with no 'Supreme Court' wording. record_before.name: Peacemakers Court (brochure description)
record_before.description: The brochure lists ideal cases as family disputes (spouses, parents and children, extended families), community disputes (nuisance, trespass, disorderly conduct, disturbing the peace), financial disputes (personal debts, breach of contract) and individual land-use and access disputes. Sessions include one male and one female peacemaker, no lawyers, voluntary participation, and a binding resolution agreed by all parties. Guiding principles are given in English and Wampanoag.
record_before.relationship_to_court: Part of the Tribal Judiciary; the Chief Judge of the Supreme Court supervises the Peacemakers Court and the appointed peacemakers.
record_before.enforcement: The final decision is agreed upon by all parties and described as binding.
record_before.note: The numeral 8 is part of the Wampanoag spelling as printed and is kept exactly. Language tag wam (Wampanoag) assigned because the brochure gives Wampanoag terms beside English; the brochure does not name the language. Supervision detail from the Tribe's About Peacemakers Court page. Peacemaker names printed in the brochure are not recorded.

apply.relationship_to_court: Part of the Tribal Judiciary. A person may ask the Court Clerk for peacemaking before filing a lawsuit, or a party to a pending District Court civil case may ask the judge to send it to peacemaking; the other party may decline, in which case the case stays in court, and criminal matters are excluded. The Chief Judge appoints one male and one female peacemaker from a roll certified by the Judiciary Committee and appointed by the Tribal Council; peacemakers serve under the Chief Judge's direction and supervision and report results to the District Court or Chief Judge (Chapter 3, Secs. 2-4).
apply.enforcement: The brochure calls the final decision binding and agreed by all parties; Chapter 3 Sec. 2(f) says an agreement reached is a final decision without appeal, and Sec. 2(b) says the Peacemaker Court cannot compel anyone to take part. The texts read do not describe a separate enforcement mechanism.

records.document: Tribal-State Compact for Control of Class III Video Games of Chance on the Prairie Island Sioux Community Reservation in Minnesota; Federal Register notice April 2, 1990 (compact executed 11/15/89)
records.locator: Sections 3.1, 4.5-4.6 (Prairie Island video games of chance compact); whole text searched for arbitration and mediation (none)
records.quote: Video games of chance believed to be non-complying shall be so designated, in writing, by the Commissioner of the Department of Public Safety.
records.findings: The text is the Prairie Island Sioux Community's compact, not the Minnesota Chippewa Tribe's (the MCT is not a party; its member bands have their own compacts, none in project files). Section 4.6 matches the record: within 5 days of the Commissioner's written designation the Community must accept the finding and remove the games, or contest it by arranging independent test-laboratory inspection within three days, or by suing in federal district court (then the National Indian Gaming Commission, then a court of competent jurisdiction if jurisdiction is declined); games found non-complying are removed from play. No arbitration or mediation anywhere. Record therefore sits on the wrong nation; this cannot be fixed by field edits (needs moving to the Prairie Island profile or dropping). Agree with first reading.

records.document: Nez Perce Tribal Code, Title 1 General Provisions, Chapter 1-8 Peacemaker Court (Chapter adopted by NPTEC 06/25/19)
records.locator: Title 1, Chapter 1-8 Peacemaker Court, sections 1-8-1 to 1-8-11
records.quote: The purpose of the Peacemaker Court is to provide a voluntary forum for the practice of traditional, non-adversarial Nez Perce methods of dispute and conflict resolution
records.findings: Read 1-8-1 to 1-8-11 in full. The Peacemaker Court is a division of the Tribal Court; cases reach it by order of a Tribal Court or specialty court judge with party agreement (1-8-8: adult non-serious criminal matters, juvenile delinquency, civil matters except contract disputes, specialty court referrals), and can be sent back; it cannot compel attendance (1-8-9). A resulting agreement can be submitted as a Peacemaking Resolution and entered by the Tribal Court as a judgment enforceable like any other (1-8-10). Section 1-8-11 allows minor matters not before a court by written request of all parties and all peacemakers, with agreements not enforceable in Tribal Court. Locator 'Nez Perce Tribe' is not a section and the note is out of date. The record has no summary. The first reading missed the court-entered judgment point in 1-8-10 and the 1-8-8 case list; added here.

first_reading.locator: Title 1, Chapter 1-8 Peacemaker Court, §§1-8-1 (establishment and purpose), 1-8-2 (definitions incl. The last item is narrower than the note suggests: 1-8-11 covers only minor disputes such as nuisance, animal trespass, and non-violent disorderly conduct, requires written consent of all parties and of all peacemakers, and says those agreements are not enforceable in Tribal Court. The record's locator 'Nez Perce Tribe' is not a section, and the note says the provision was not read, which is now out of date. The adoption date is printed on the chapter.

apply.summary: Establishes the Nez Perce Peacemaker Court as a division of the Tribal Court, a voluntary, non-adversarial forum using traditional Nez Perce methods that does not assign fault. A Tribal Court or specialty court judge may send it adult non-serious criminal matters, juvenile delinquency matters, and civil matters other than contract disputes, with the parties' agreement, and the case can be sent back if unresolved. It cannot compel anyone to attend. An agreement can be submitted as a Peacemaking Resolution and entered by the Tribal Court as a judgment enforced like any other; minor disputes outside the courts can also be heard on written request of all parties, but those agreements are not enforceable in Tribal Court.

records.document: 1995 Class III Gaming Compact between the Nez Perce Tribe and the State of Idaho, dated August 22, 1995; approved by the Department of the Interior October 1995
records.locator: Article 21 (Dispute Resolution), 21.1-21.3; Article 6 (6.1-6.3); 2003 addendum and 2008 compact searched for dispute terms (none)
records.quote: either party may pursue binding arbitration to enforce or resolve disputes concerning the provisions of this Compact.
records.findings: The record was built from the Coeur d'Alene 1993 compact; this nation's own 1995 compact has the same procedure: written notice, meeting within 10 working days, after 60 days either party may pursue binding arbitration, three arbitrators selected by the American Arbitration Association, decision within 120 days of selection unless extended, no judicial review, and the decision has the effect of part of the compact (21.2). 21.3 preserves other methods (mediation, mini-trials) by mutual agreement only. The parenthetical that Article 6 disputes follow their own procedure is unsupported: Article 6 (authorized gaming; six-monthly meetings) has no procedure; 21.1 and 21.2 just say 'except as provided in Article 6'. The 2003 addendum and 2008 lottery compact have no dispute article. Agree with first reading. Lead session: the 1995 compact is named as the version described on purpose; the 2008 compact listed as its replacement covers only the Idaho State Lottery on the reservation and has no dispute resolution article.

first_reading.locator: Article 21 (Dispute Resolution), §§21.1-21.3; Article 6 (§§6.1-6.3) checked for its own procedure
first_reading.quote: either party may pursue binding arbitration to enforce or resolve disputes concerning the provisions of this Compact.
first_reading.findings: The record's source is the Coeur d'Alene Tribe's 1993 compact, not the Nez Perce compact, so the record's source and as_of are for another nation. The Nez Perce 1995 compact in the project files does support the summary: notice, a 10-working-day meeting, then after 60 days binding arbitration by three arbitrators selected by the American Arbitration Association, with no judicial review. But the parenthetical that Article 6 disputes 'follow that article's own procedure' is not supported: Article 6 (6.1-6.3) contains no dispute procedure, and Article 21 simply excludes Article 6. The 2008 Nez Perce Lottery compact (the record's deemed-approved status is from 2008) has no dispute-resolution article at all, which the summary should say.

proposed_changes.summary: Under Article 21 of the 1995 compact, a party alleging non-compliance serves written notice; the parties meet within ten working days; if the dispute is not resolved within sixty days after notice, either party may pursue binding arbitration before three arbitrators selected by the American Arbitration Association, with no judicial review. Article 21 is subject to Article 6, which sets no separate dispute procedure. The 2008 Nez Perce lottery compact has no dispute-resolution article.

record_before.dispute_resolution_summary: After written notice the parties meet within 10 working days, and if the dispute is not resolved within 60 days either party may pursue binding arbitration before a three-member panel selected by the American Arbitration Association, with no judicial review of the decision (disputes under Article 6 follow that article's own procedure).

apply.dispute_resolution_summary: Under Article 21 of the 1995 compact, a party alleging non-compliance serves written notice and the parties meet within 10 working days. If the dispute is not resolved within 60 days of the notice, either party may pursue binding arbitration before three arbitrators selected by the American Arbitration Association, who may declare rights and grant relief permitted by law; decision is due within 120 days of their selection, there is no judicial review, and the decision has the effect of part of the compact. Once arbitration is noticed the matter cannot be litigated in court. The parties may agree to other methods such as mediation. The 2003 addendum and 2008 lottery compact have no dispute-resolution article.

records.findings: Read all of 50.20. records.quote: If parties to a dispute agree in writing or orally before the Tribal Court, a Peacemaker may arbitrate a dispute by hearing all sides of it and then issuing a decision.
records.findings: Checked each claim: department of the Tribal Court under the chief judge (103); purpose language (101); listed matters and $1,500 limit (104); disputes resolved under the Code may be approved as judgments and are enforceable (105(c)); attorneys barred (106); arbitration on agreement with a decision having judgment effect on entry and civil appeal (202(f)); judge appoints with parties' concurrence (305(a)); $10 judgment fee (309); civil transfer by written stipulation or good cause (602); criminal transfer limits (603) and probation condition (604); transfer on condition with stay and reassumption (605). Details the record omits but that do not make it wrong: the Court may order mediation but a peacemaker is primarily a mediator and decides only if all parties agree (105(b)); an unresolved matter returns to the court after 30 days or agreed time (105(b)); peacemakers can compel persons to meet (202(d)). Juvenile as a case type is not named explicitly in 104 (covered by 'parent and child' and 'any other matter'). Record supported.

first_reading.locator: Title 7 Peacemaker Code, Sections 101-107, 201-205, 301-309, 401-406, 501-503, 601-605, 701-702 (whole code read); 202(f), 203(a), 305(a) central to the record

record_before.name: Peacemaker Court of the Northern Arapaho Nation
record_before.description: A department of the Tribal Court intended to give formal support, structure and enforcement to traditional Northern Arapaho methods of resolving disputes through mediation and traditional ways without judges or lawyers. If parties agree in writing or orally, a peacemaker may hear all sides of a dispute and issue a decision.
record_before.legal_basis: Northern Arapaho Code, Title 7. Peacemaker Code, Sections 101-702
record_before.relationship_to_court: Established as a department of the Tribal Court; a judge may appoint a peacemaker with the parties' concurrence, and civil or criminal cases may be transferred on stipulation or for good cause, with a stay of court proceedings that the court may lift on breach of a condition.
record_before.enforcement: Resolved disputes may be approved as judgments or orders of the Tribal Court and are enforceable; if all parties agree, a peacemaker may hear all sides and issue a decision that takes effect as a court judgment when entered, appealable under civil appeal rules.
record_before.note: Listed matters (Sec. 104) include marital and family strife, parent-child disputes, minor neighbor disputes, alcohol use by family or neighbors, and minor community business transactions of $1,500 or less. Attorneys barred from proceedings (Sec. 106). Criminal transfers limited to cases without injury, with victim consent, or victimless offenses, or as a probation condition (Sec. 603-604). $10 fee for a judgment or protective order (Sec. 309). Folded on 2026-11-22 from a separate forum record for the same text (review queue item 5). Agreed decisions rest on Northern Arapaho Code, Title 7, Section 202(f). The decision is submitted to the Tribal Court for entry as a written judgment, and it takes the effect of a court judgment once entered; appealable under the Tribal Court's civil appeal rules.

records.locator: Chapter 5.3 Labor Relations, section 5.3-14(A)-(C) Resolution of unfair labor practice charges
records.quote: When a question arises as to whether an unfair labor practice was committed, the party charging the unfair labor practice charge may file a written request for arbitration to the party charged with the violation.
records.findings: Read 5.3-14 in full. Charging party files a written request for arbitration within 60 days of the event; arbitration happens only if both parties agree; arbitrator mutually agreed or chosen by the FMCS procedure (National Academy of Arbitrators member), fees shared equally; arbitrator applies tribal law, cannot modify the chapter, may fashion a remedy (back wages limited); written decision final and binding except a 10-day appeal to the Nottawaseppi Supreme Court for errors of law or fact (B); if both parties do not agree within 30 days of the demand, the Tribal Court has jurisdiction, with a complaint due within 90 days of the violation (C). Record's citation 'Sec.13.01' is the NILL contents heading (2014 index) and the code now numbers it 5.3-14; the first reading's proposed summary is accurate and I add the 90-day filing limit and the correct section reference. Source link should be the eCode360 page.

The 2009 and 2016 amendments do not touch Section 7 (they say unamended provisions remain in force). records.findings: Read all 18 rules; the NARF PDF's table of contents and Rules 1-3 match. Peacemaker Court is part of the Nation Court system under the Chief Trial Judge (2). The Chief Trial Judge appoints a peacemaker in any matter deemed appropriate or where parties request it (3(a), 4); attorneys barred unless witnesses or parties (3(c)); peacemakers may compel witnesses by subpoena, enforced by contempt only on the peacemaker's request (3(b), 13); peacemakers cannot decide a dispute unless all parties agree in writing, and then the decision has the effect of a court judgment when entered (6); transfer needs written consent of all parties, any party can block it and can withdraw consent at any time (11); the parties' agreement becomes the court's judgment and is enforced like any Nation Court order (14). apply.summary: Establishes the Peacemaker Court as part of the Oneida Nation Court system under the Chief Trial Judge. The Chief Trial Judge appoints a peacemaker when a party requests one or in any matter deemed appropriate, but a case is transferred only with the written consent of all parties, any of whom may block the transfer or withdraw consent and return the case to the Trial Court. Attorneys are barred unless they are witnesses or parties. Peacemakers use Nation traditional ways, may compel witnesses by subpoena, and may decide a dispute only if all parties agree in writing. The parties' agreement, or such a decision, becomes a judgment of the Nation Court enforced like any other order.

apply.summary: In a custody, placement or visitation case the Court may refer the parents to peacemaking or mediation only if they agree, and not where attending would cause undue hardship or endanger a party (evidence of domestic abuse is considered); the Court pays when it refers. Peacemakers are those recognized by the Tribe's Cultural Heritage Department or the Court, and the parties choose the type; mediators need 25 hours of training or 3 years of experience plus domestic violence training. An agreement is written, certified by the peacemaker or mediator and submitted to the Court as a stipulation in the order; the Court may reject it if not in the child's best interest, giving written reasons. If there is no agreement the Court is told and the parties may return to peacemaking before trial. After an order, the Court may also refer a parent to peacemaking or mediation to resolve problems (705.7-5).

apply.summary: Sets who may serve as a Trial Court peacemaker or mediator and how they are used. Outsiders apply to the Court Administrator, pass a background check and are approved by the judges after an interview. Before being used a person must show understanding of the role (training, prior Trial Court work, recognition by the Cultural Heritage Department or another jurisdiction, or other means the Court accepts). The Trial Court may refer parties under 8 O.C. 801.6-2, keeps the list and selects from it, and no one with an interest in the case may be appointed without the parties' consent. Peacemakers must keep cases confidential, avoid conflicts and give the Court a written update within three business days of a session; the Trial Court hears complaints and may discipline, including removal from the list; pay is at a reasonable rate set by the Court, and nothing is paid for work by a full-time Judge.

records.findings: Read both versions. Scan Sec. 3A says at least 12 peacemakers (record's wording); the 2024 code says at least 7 and no more than 12, adds a Community Court and renames the appeal body. Record's decision rules are supported by scan Secs. 7-8; 2024 Ch. 2 Sec. 17D has circle decisions written as Orders of the Tribal Court, failing consensus back to a hearing panel. Record's enforcement left out what happens after a decision: Ch. 2 Secs. 19-22 give 30 days to comply, proof of compliance to the Clerk, and failure to comply with an Order or Consensus Agreement is contempt, with seizure and sale of property after 30 days' notice. Also missing: how a case enters (Ch. 2 Sec. 14: petition to the Clerk, or referral or transfer from another court; Review Meeting of at least two peacemakers) and appeal (Ch. 3: petition within 30 days, Court of Appeals has discretion to take it; uphold, order rehearing or dismiss). Chapter 2 Secs. 3-13 and 15-16 not read. Participation not stated as voluntary; left as recorded.

own_term.name: Keex’ Kwaan
own_term.translation: Kake (the code uses it as the Tribe's own name for Kake, Alaska)

record_before.description: The Tribe's court, in which its judicial powers are vested, organized as peacemaking: a standing pool of at least twelve peacemakers (Council members and resident citizens) sitting in panels of three, Peacemaking Circles led by a Keeper of the Circle recognized by the Council, a Court of Appeals, and other courts the Council may create. The code applies written tribal laws and Keex’ Kwaan cultural values and traditions, and states that the ancestors formed the clan of Guwakaan, the Deer People, as the process of peacemaking, which no moiety claims.
record_before.legal_basis: Keex’ Kwaan Judicial Peacemaking Code, Chapter 1, Sections 1-12 (under Article V of the OVK Constitution)
record_before.relationship_to_court: The peacemaking court is the Tribe's judiciary; a review team of peacemakers decides whether to take a petition and whether to use a circle or a panel.
record_before.enforcement: Panels decide by consensus when possible and otherwise by majority vote; circles decide by consensus written as Consensus Agreements of the court, with set follow-up; if a circle cannot reach consensus the case goes to a panel.
record_before.note: Read from OCR of a scanned copy. Peacemakers may consult Elders and Council members (Section 9). NARF notes the code includes a Peacemaker Appellate Court and a Circle Peacemaking flow chart. as_of is NARF posting year.

apply.description: The Tribe's court, in which its judicial powers are vested, organized as peacemaking. Under the July 2024 code the system has a Standing Peacemaking Court (a pool of at least 7 and no more than 12 peacemakers, of whom 7 may be OVK Council members and the rest resident citizens, sitting in panels of three), a Circle Court led by a Keeper of the Circle, a Community Court of at least two judges, a Court of Appeals, and other courts the Council may create. The code applies written tribal laws and Keex' Kwaan cultural values and traditions, and says the ancestors formed the clan of Guwakaan, the Deer People, as the process of peacemaking, which no moiety claims. The earlier scanned copy said a pool of at least 12.
apply.legal_basis: Keex' Kwaan Peacemaking Code (adopted July 2024), Ch. 1 (1.01.010-1.03.150), Ch. 2 (Court Procedures) and Ch. 3 (Court of Appeals), under Article V of the OVK Constitution
apply.relationship_to_court: The peacemaking court is the Tribe's judiciary. A case generally starts with a Petition to Use the Tribal Court filed with the Court Clerk, or by referral or transfer from another court; the Clerk calls a Review Meeting of at least two peacemakers, who decide whether to take the case and whether to use a circle or a three-peacemaker panel.
apply.enforcement: Panels decide by consensus when possible and otherwise by majority vote. Circles decide by consensus, written as Orders (Consensus Agreements) of the Tribal Court, and a circle that cannot agree sends the case back to a hearing panel. Orders must be carried out within 30 days unless the order says otherwise, with proof of compliance filed with the Clerk, who reports failures to the Court. Failure to comply with an Order or Consensus Agreement is contempt of court, and the Tribal Court may seize the person's personal property and, after 30 days' notice, sell it. A person may petition the Court of Appeals within 30 days of an Order; the Court of Appeals decides whether to take the case and may uphold, order a rehearing or dismiss.
apply.note: Read in full on 2026-11-23 from page images (Keex' Kwaan Peacemaking Code, Organized Village of Kake, Adopted July 2024 (earlier scanned copy undated)). records.locator: Chapter 4 (Kake Youth Circle Peacemaking), Sections 1-13, printed pp. 35-44
records.quote: The Consensus Agreement ordered by the Kake Youth Circle Peacemaking shall be designed to help and heal victims, wrongdoers, and the Village of Kake.
records.findings: Quote found (Sec. 1). Description is supported. Enforcement is incomplete: Sec. 12 gives 7 days to file Proof of Compliance with mentor sign-off; if not met the Youth Coordinator may schedule another Circle or report the failure to the regular court and schedule a Contempt of Court hearing; Sec. 8J says a non-complying person may be brought before the Circle again or the case referred to the Kake District Court. Entry missing from the record: a case starts by Petition from anyone (Sec. 5A) or referral from a state judge, law enforcement officer or another tribal court (5B), reviewed by two youth and staff; a served wrongdoer who does not appear may be fetched by a designated adult (Sec. 10); the Kake District Court of Alaska may take over a case at any time (Sec. 3). Appeal in Sec. 13: notice within 10 days to a three-peacemaker panel. Participation is not stated as voluntary; left as court-referred.

first_reading.locator: Chapter 4, Sections 1-13 (printed pp. 34-44); the 2024 Nation version's printed p. 41 checked and matches
first_reading.quote: The Consensus Agreement ordered by the Kake Youth Circle Peacemaking shall be designed to help and heal victims, wrongdoers, and the Village of Kake.
first_reading.findings: The youth circle is part of the Tribal Court system (Sec. 2), covers ages 8 to 18 (Sec. 3), and ends in Consensus Agreements meant to help and heal victims, wrongdoers and the village (Sec. 1, 11). The options are community service, restitution, apologies, essays and presentations, events or fundraisers, counseling by professionals, Elders or peers, substance-abuse sessions and talking circles, and traditional activities (Sec. 11 A-H). Proof of compliance, follow-up with referral to Kake District Court, and appeal to a three-peacemaker panel within 10 days (Sec. 8J, 12, 13) also appear. Cases start by petition from anyone or by referral from state judges, police or other tribal courts (Sec. 5), and a served wrongdoer may be fetched by a designated adult (Sec. 10), so 'court-referred' is supported.

apply.description: Part of the OVK Tribal Court system, for youth aged 8 to 18 in health, safety and welfare matters (alcohol and drugs, vandalism, trespass, theft, bullying, harassment, disorderly conduct, tardiness, truancy, curfew). It encourages responsible choices, involves youth in decisions about peers' problems, and produces Consensus Agreements designed to help and heal victims, wrongdoers and the Village. Options include community service, restitution, apologies, essays and presentations, events or fundraisers, counseling by professionals, Elders or peers, substance abuse sessions, talking circles and traditional activities. The Kake District Court of Alaska may take or take over a case at any time.
apply.relationship_to_court: Established by the OVK Council as part of the Tribal Court system, with a youth coordinator, youth panel and mentors. A case begins by petition from anyone to the Youth Coordinator, or by referral from a state court judge, a law enforcement officer or another tribal court; the Youth Coordinator with two youth reviews it and decides whether to hold a Circle.
apply.enforcement: Mentors oversee the Consensus Agreement. The party files a Proof of Compliance within 7 days of completing it. On failure the Youth Coordinator may schedule another Circle or report the failure to the regular Kake Youth Circle Peacemaking court and schedule a Contempt of Court hearing; a non-complying person may also be referred to the Kake District Court (Section 8J). A youth may appeal within 10 days to a panel of three Peacemakers (Section 13).

record_before.description: An informal, flexible process in which a neutral mediator helps parties resolve their own disputes outside the adversarial process; the first step for all family-related civil cases filed in the Pascua Yaqui Tribal Court.
record_before.legal_basis: 5 PYTC Chapter 9 (Mediation), §§ 9-10, 9-30
record_before.relationship_to_court: The court clerk refers all civil cases involving families to mediation, for initial and modification proceedings; the court may decline referral on request for parental unfitness, substance abuse, mental incapacity, domestic violence, other good cause or undue delay, and a judge may refer a case at any time.
record_before.note: Mandatory case types listed: marriage, dissolution of marriage, child custody and visitation, adoption, permanent guardianship or conservatorship, paternity, child support, probate.

apply.relationship_to_court: The court clerk refers all civil cases involving families to mediation, for initial and modification proceedings; on a party's request the court may decline referral for parental unfitness, substance abuse, mental incapacity, domestic violence, other good cause or undue delay, a judge may refer a case at any time, and domestic violence, child abuse and emergency custody or protection-order cases are exempt (the court may also waive on a showing of abuse history, a stipulated settlement or good cause). A mediated agreement binds the parties once written and signed or stated on the record, but is not binding on the court until the court approves it. The court may enforce the chapter through contempt, compliance hearings or sanctions, and may impose sanctions on a party who fails to appear.

records.locator: Native Justice page: 'What is it?', 'What kinds of disputes is it for?', 'How can I be involved?'
records.quote: Circle keepers are not judges; they do not decide the outcome. Those involved in the dispute will determine their solution.
records.findings: Quote found. Description, civil case type and consequences claim are supported ('Citizens can use the Native Justice forum for civil disputes before coming to the court'; participants 'set standards... and also design the consequences if they do not'). Page also says it will be how citizens resolve disputes 'without using the Tribal Courts'. It does not say how a case is started or who runs it, and does not say the outcome is binding or enforced by the court; the record's enforcement line should say so. 'Voluntary' is an inference from 'can use' and 'encourages'.

first_reading.locator: 'What is it?', 'What kinds of disputes is it for?', 'Why is this better than using a court?', 'How can I be involved?' sections of the Native Justice page
first_reading.quote: Circle keepers are not judges; they do not decide the outcome. Those involved in the dispute will determine their solution.
first_reading.findings: The Band's own Native Justice page says the program is commonly referred to as Peacemaking and uses ceremonial traditions, talking circles and circle keepers; circle keepers facilitate and do not decide, and participants set standards and design consequences. It lists three strands (Native Justice for Court; Community Conflict and Dispute Resolution Forum; Community Education and Awareness), civil disputes for the forum with criminal cases staying in court. 'Voluntary' participation is an inference from 'Citizens can use the Native Justice forum', not a stated word; the page does not say 'required' or 'voluntary' explicitly.

record_before.name: Native Justice Community Conflict and Dispute Resolution Forum
record_before.description: Native Justice, which the Band says is commonly referred to as peacemaking, uses talking circles and circle keepers to bring people in a dispute to common ground; circle keepers facilitate but do not decide, and participants set their own solution and consequences. The program has three strands: Native Justice for Court, the Community Conflict and Dispute Resolution Forum, and Community Education and Awareness.
record_before.relationship_to_court: Citizens may use the forum for civil disputes before coming to court; the court continues to handle criminal cases and encourages use of the forum for civil disputes.
record_before.enforcement: Participants design the consequences if standards they set are not met.
record_before.note: The page says the process uses ceremonial traditions; no further detail is recorded.

apply.enforcement: Participants each set standards they are expected to keep and design the consequences if they do not. The page does not say the outcome is binding or enforced by the court.

records.document: Prairie Band Potawatomi Constitution, approved 12.6.2007 (Nation's website)
records.locator: Constitution Article VI, Sections 1-3
records.quote: Peacemakers shall be of such number as may be determined by the General Council and shall have the responsibility for mediating disputes voluntarily submitted to them by the parties.
records.findings: Quote found. Record's description and participation (voluntary) supported. Section 2: peacemakers selected by members at a General Council meeting, removed by their appointing authority; Sec. 3: power necessary to mediate disputes, procedures defined by Nation law. Text sets no subject-matter limit, so case types are unspecified; kept the record's values rather than inventing a vocabulary entry. Text says nothing about whether a peacemaking outcome is binding; first reading omitted this. NARF note's foreclosure and attorney-ban claims are not in Article VI, as the record already says.

first_reading.locator: Constitution Article VI (Dispute Resolution System), Sections 1-3 (same text in tribal-law/documents/b7f92d971c7c30a4032c.pdf, sha256 matches the 4674280c... capture)
first_reading.quote: Peacemakers shall be of such number as may be determined by the General Council and shall have the responsibility for mediating disputes voluntarily submitted to them by the parties.
first_reading.findings: Article VI confirms a separate mediating branch, Peacemakers Circle, separate from the Judicial Council; peacemakers are selected by members at a General Council meeting and mediate disputes voluntarily submitted by the parties; procedures are set by Nation law. The record's case types ('civil', 'other') are not stated: the text sets no subject-matter limit on what peacemakers mediate. The NARF note's foreclosure of District Court proceedings and attorney ban are not in Article VI (no matching text in the constitution).

case_types: any dispute voluntarily submitted by the parties (no case-type limit stated)

record_before.name: Peacemakers Circle
record_before.description: A separate mediating branch established in the constitution's Dispute Resolution System; peacemakers are selected by the Nation's members at a General Council meeting and are responsible for mediating disputes voluntarily submitted by the parties.
record_before.legal_basis: Constitution of the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation, Article VI (Dispute Resolution System), Sections 1-3
record_before.relationship_to_court: Established alongside, and separate from, the Judicial Council (District Court, Court of Appeals and Employment Disputes Tribunal); procedures are to be defined by Nation law.
record_before.note: NARF's summary adds that the provision covers foreclosure of further District Court proceedings and an attorney ban; those details were not located in the Article VI text reviewed and may be in implementing law.

apply.enforcement: The constitution does not say whether a peacemaking result is binding or enforced; it gives peacemakers power to mediate and leaves procedures to Nation law.
apply.note: Read in full on 2026-11-23 (Prairie Band Potawatomi Constitution, approved 12.6.2007 (Nation's website)). Article VI read in full (Nation's constitution, approved 2007-12-06). first_reading.quote: The Employment Disputes Tribunal shall be comprised of five (5) magistrates and shall have the responsibility for deciding all government employment related disputes.
first_reading.findings: Article VI supports the summary: a five-magistrate Employment Disputes Tribunal within the Judicial Council, deciding all government employment related disputes; two magistrates appointed by the Tribal Council, two by employees, one by the other four. The District Court's jurisdiction excludes those disputes (Sec. 1 and 3). 'Required' participation is an inference from its adjudicative role, consistent with the text. The record's note calls the kind 'employment-tribunal' but the kind field says 'administrative-adjudication'; the note is stale.

First reading's summary right but left out: a patron who does not request an investigation within seven days loses any claim; an operation that fails to give timely notice faces regulatory penalty and the patron's seven days run from actual notice; the hearing may be waived by both sides; the Board's decision is a final action effective on receipt; Pueblo Court review under 14-1-14 is limited to the Board record and reverses only if arbitrary, capricious or contrary to law, and is the final appellate body. The 2018 codified version in the record's NILL index was not seen.

first_reading.findings: The nation's gaming control ordinance (as amended, approved by NIGC on 2013-07-09) contains Section 14-1-9 'Dispute Resolution', so the title and citation are supported. apply.citation: Pueblo of Laguna Gaming Control Ordinance, Section 14-1-9 (Dispute Resolution), as amended by Resolution No. 27-13 and approved by the NIGC July 9, 2013
apply.summary: Handles a patron's complaint that a gaming operation or management contractor refused to pay alleged winnings. If under $500, the operation tells the patron in writing of the right to ask the Gaming Control Board to investigate within seven days; if $500 or more, it notifies the Board within 48 hours and gives the patron a copy with the same right. A patron who does not ask in time loses any claim. The Board investigates and holds a hearing (unless both sides waive it), then issues a written decision, which is a final action. Either side may appeal to the Pueblo Court within 14 days of receiving it; review is limited to the Board's record, and the Board is reversed only if arbitrary, capricious or contrary to law (Section 14-1-14). An operation that fails to notify the Board on time faces a regulatory penalty.

records.quote: The court may appoint a member of the Community who is qualified by experience and temperament to act as a tribal elder and conduct the hearing
records.findings: Read Sec. 11-31 in the community's own code. It matches the record (extended families help the juvenile court with juvenile offender, incorrigibility and dependency problems using Pima and Maricopa customs; the court may appoint an elder to conduct the hearing and make written disposition recommendations). Missing from the record: the case gets there by the court's own motion or the motion of a parent, guardian or the Community before a merits hearing (11-31(c)), after the court inquires into applicability and suitability (d); the hearing is informal but must give family members and the child a chance to be heard, allow evidence, and exclude the public (e); the court, not the elder, enters judgment, noting that this procedure was used, tries to build the extended family into its order and may require family members to perform acts or services, and appeal lies under 11-29 (f). Participation is not voluntary-by-consent in the text; the court orders attendance of extended family members.

apply.description: Alternative juvenile court procedure that uses the extended families of the Community, and the customs and traditions of the Pima and Maricopa peoples, to resolve juvenile offender, incorrigibility and dependency problems. Before a hearing on the merits the court, on its own motion or on motion of a parent, guardian or the Community, may order the case heard this way after inquiring into whether it is applicable and suitable. The court may appoint a Community member qualified to act as a tribal elder to conduct the informal hearing, and may order extended family members to attend.
apply.relationship_to_court: The appointed elder makes written recommendations of disposition to the court. records.document: Sauk-Suiattle Indian Tribe Gaming Ordinance, adopted by Resolution 11/29/99 (Nov. 19, 1999), Wayback Machine copy filed Nov. 23, 2026
records.locator: § 7.3 (printed pages 9-10)
records.quote: Patrons who have complaints against the gaming establishment shall have as their sole remedy the right to file a petition for relief with the Gaming Commission.
records.findings: Section 7.3 makes a written petition to the Gaming Commission the patron's sole remedy; disputes with a management contractor or its employees also go to the Commission, which is the exclusive remedy for patron complaints. The Commission may let the petitioner present evidence, decides in a timely fashion, and its decisions are final when issued. Claims must be submitted within thirty days of the occurrence, and recovery is capped at $10,000 per occurrence and $20,000 per patron in any twelve-month period. Read from the page images (printed pages 9-10) because the text layer is an OCR scan.

records.document: Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians Tribal Code, Chapter 36: Juvenile Code (Res. 2000-27; amended through Res. 2020-101, May 5, 2020)
records.locator: Tribal Code Chapter 36 (Juvenile Code), Section 36.405(1)-(4), pp. 36-21 to 36-22
records.quote: The Sault Ste. Marie Chippewa Tribal Court shall promulgate the guidelines governing Peacemaking.
records.findings: Quote found. Description, case types and participation supported by 36.405. First reading marked confirmed, but the record still says it was inferred from NCORJ and has no enforcement. The text gives one consequence: the Committee may ask the Prosecutor to file a formal petition (36.405(3); a petition under 36.406 starts formal juvenile proceedings) if the case plan has not been substantially followed. Entry routes are in 36.405(2) and (4): prosecutor presents cases to the Committee; Tribal Court referral; members requesting it voluntarily. Section does not say peacemaking agreements are otherwise binding.

first_reading.locator: Tribal Code Chapter 36 (Juvenile Code), Subchapter IV, Section 36.405 (1)-(4), pp. 36-21 to 36-22
first_reading.quote: 36.405 Bekaadziiwiin (Peaceful Life). (1) The Sault Ste. Marie Chippewa Tribal Court shall promulgate the guidelines governing Peacemaking.
first_reading.findings: Section 36.405 confirms the record: the Tribal Court promulgates peacemaking guidelines; the Tribal Prosecutor presents cases to the Tribal Peacemaking Committee, which may decline action, refer the matter to Bekaadziiwiin, develop a case plan, or refer to the Juvenile Division; the Committee may ask for a formal petition if the case plan is not substantially followed. Peacemakers may hear juvenile offenses, juvenile status offenses, cases referred by the Tribal Court, and cases from tribal members who voluntarily request peacemaking. The 'diversion' label in the record is the record's characterization of these pre-petition options; the code does not use the word.

records.document: Tribal-State Compact for Control of Class III Video Games of Chance on the Shakopee Mdewakanton Sioux Community Reservation in Minnesota, executed Oct. 20, 1989 / Dec. 1989, Federal Register notice April 2, 1990
records.quote: contest the finding of non-compliance by so notifying the Commissioner of Public Safety in writing
records.findings: Quote found. The Shakopee compact itself has Sec. 4.6, matching the record's description; no arbitration or mediation clause. The record's source and note (Prairie Island text, 'nation-specific text not checked') are out of date. Missing details: the Commissioner of Public Safety designates a machine non-complying in writing; within 5 days the Community must accept the finding or contest it; contest routes are written notice plus inspection by an independent gaming test laboratory within 3 days (a lab finding of non-compliance means permanent removal unless modified), or an action in federal district court, then the National Indian Gaming Commission if the court declines jurisdiction, then a court of competent jurisdiction. Sec. 4.6 preserves IGRA rights and remedies; Sec. 2.2 treats a renegotiation request as a request to negotiate under IGRA (180 days); Sec. 7 reserves IGRA 11(d)(7) rights. Text-layer is noisy OCR but legible. Lead session: the 1990 video games of chance compact is named as the version described on purpose; the 1991 compact listed as its replacement is, by the compact history's summary, a different text whose dispute provision is Section 10 (Effect of Breach), which this record does not describe.

records.locator: Chapter 1, Sections 1.1.8 to 1.1.11
records.quote: The Traditional Peacemaking Court shall have original jurisdiction over a dispute if all parties involved agree to peacemaking and request to appear before the Traditional Peacemaking Court.
records.findings: Quote found at 1.1.8(D)(2)(a). Every NARF point is in the text. The first reading's note leaves out how cases enter and enforcement: referral by a Tribal Court judge with all parties' written consent (1.1.10), joint request to the Clerk with a consent declaration (1.1.9), statute (including juvenile delinquency and educational neglect), and a civil trial judge may order at least one hour of peacemaking without consent (1.1.10(E)). Peacemakers cannot decide unless all parties agree in writing (1.1.8(G)) and cannot compel appearance unless another law says so (1.1.8(E)).
