apply.title: Sokaogon Chippewa Community Code, Ch. 1 Sections 1.1.8-1.1.11 - Traditional Peacemaking Court
apply.citation: Sokaogon Chippewa Community Codes, Chapter 1 (Tribal Governance), Sections 1.1.8 to 1.1.11
apply.summary: Creates the Traditional Peacemaking Court as a branch of the Tribal Court, staffed by Tribal Judges who serve as peacemakers. A case gets there when a Tribal Court judge refers it with all parties' written consent (not hunting, fishing, traffic or child-protection cases), when all parties jointly ask the Tribal Court Clerk, when a statute provides (including juvenile delinquency and educational neglect), or, in a civil case, when the trial judge orders at least one hour of peacemaking even without consent. The court cannot compel anyone to take part unless another law says so, and peacemakers mediate and cannot decide unless all parties agree in writing. Each party pays $25; sessions are confidential, and results go to the Tribal Court in writing when it referred the case. An agreement has the effect of a court judgment when the Tribal Court enters it, which it does only if the conditions in Section 1.1.11 are met; if there is no agreement or it is breached, Tribal Court proceedings continue.

records.locator: Section XIV (Dispute Resolution), A-D, compact pages 37-38
records.quote: The parties shall meet and confer in a good faith attempt to resolve the dispute through negotiation not later than twenty (20) business days from receipt of the notice.
records.findings: Quote exact. Record summary is accurate as far as it goes but leaves out parts of XIV: arbitration (B(3)) has a Tribe/State Gaming Agency-selected arbitrator, hearing within 14 business days of naming, final decision within one year, may impose fines and award equitable relief, and the decision is final only for the non-judicial phase and subject to judicial review; section XIV(C) gives a limited waiver of sovereign immunity for the suits in XIV(B); XIV(D) sends any dispute arising under the compact to XIV. The date 2021-09-01 cannot be confirmed from the text: the approval letter is dated August 2021, the Federal Register notice that the project holds for 2021-09-01 (2021-18821) is the Tulalip compact amendment, not Stillaguamish. The BIA file name carries 2021.09.01, which suggests Federal Register publication that day, so I leave as_of unchanged but it is not verified from the Stillaguamish text. records.document: Choctaw Nation Peacemaking Act (7-page copy); no enactment date printed
records.locator: Choctaw Nation Peacemaking Act, sections 1-18 (read in full)
records.quote: The purpose of Choctaw Nation Peacemakers Act is to provide a forum for the use of traditional Choctaw methods of peacemaking to resolve disputes in a fair, informal, and inexpensive manner.
records.findings: Quote exact. First reader's section list holds, but with two cautions: Section 8, headed 'Use of tribal traditions and customary law', is in fact the written request procedure for asking the District Court for a peacemaker, so the NARF phrase about 'tribal customary law' rests only on the heading; use of customs and traditions is Section 7. The first reading also left out entry and enforcement: referral is by District Court order on a party's motion (objection or no response within 15 working days defeats it) or on the court's own motion, and a joint motion must be granted, with all parties consenting; peacemaker cannot force a result or adjudicate (s.5); signed agreement and proposed dismissal order go to the District Court, which endorses it as a final, non-appealable order (s.11(D)) enforceable like other District Court orders (s.13); if no agreement the case returns to the court (s.4, s.11(F)). Section 4 says peacemakers have jurisdiction if all parties agree to be bound by the peacemaker's decision, which sits oddly with s.5; I report both.

records.document: Tulalip Tribes Resolution 2024-473, Amendment to Tulalip Tribal Code 2.25 Adding 2.25.200 Enacting Alternative Court Code; adopted October 4, 2024; accepted by Puget Sound Agency Superintendent October 15, 2024
records.locator: Resolution 2024-473, Section 1 and Attachment One/Two (TTC 2.25.200 Alternative Courts), subsections (1)-(7)
records.quote: the Court will defer acceptance and entry of the guilty
records.findings: Text layer is OCR but legible. Record's summary is accurate (Wellness Court and MAP Program, Steering Committee, Prosecutor's plea-agreement offer, deferred entry of guilty plea, relaxed rules of evidence). The provision sits in Chapter 2.25 Criminal Procedures and sets up therapeutic criminal courts for defendants charged with crimes (substance use, serious mental illness); it provides no mediation, peacemaking or process for resolving a dispute between parties, so it is not dispute resolution as this dataset uses the term. Close call: if the project counts court diversion programs as ADR (it keeps the Tulalip Elders Panel), keep it as kind other with this summary. Entry: prosecutor offer in plea agreement or probation-revocation resolution, plus acceptance by the alternative court team; termination leads to formal plea acceptance and sentencing.

first_reading.locator: Resolution 2024-473, Section 1 and Attachment One (TTC 2.25.200 Alternative Courts): subsections (1) Purpose, (2) Steering Committee, (3) Jurisdiction, pretrial and probation diversion plea and deferral, (7) Rules of Evidence and Procedure. The text layer is OCR and partly garbled.
first_reading.quote: the Court will defer acceptance and entry of the guilty
first_reading.findings: The summary is accurate: TTC 2.25.200 establishes the Healing to Wellness Court and the Mental Wellness Alternatives (MAP) Program, creates an Alternative Courts Steering Committee, lets the Prosecutor offer these courts in a plea agreement, has the court defer acceptance and entry of the guilty plea, and relaxes rules of evidence. But these are criminal problem-solving courts for defendants with substance-use or serious mental illness issues, not a process for resolving disputes between parties. The record's own note says they are not peacemaking. The record is marked read-in-full in the batch only because of the earlier summary-tool read; this is now a full read of the PDF.

records.locator: Yurok Tribal Code Title 9, Ch. 9.20, section 9.20.010(a)-(d)
records.quote: The chief executive office or general manager of the gaming facility shall attempt to mediate or resolve such complaints.
records.findings: Read the section in full; quote exact (text has 'office' for 'officer'). Steps: written complaint to facility CEO/general manager who attempts to mediate or resolve; within 14 days an unsatisfied complainant may file with the Gaming Commission, which decides validity within 30 days of receipt and orders appropriate remedies; appeal to Yurok Tribal Court within 30 days, which has jurisdiction whether or not the person is a member, and its decision is final. The record's 'citation' is the chapter heading only. First reading omitted that the Commission can order remedies.

first_reading.findings: The record's title '9.20 Dispute Resolution' is the chapter heading, which is accurate, but the citation '9.20 Dispute Resolution' is not a section. The operative text is section 9.20.010: a gaming-public complaint goes to the gaming facility CEO or general manager, who attempts mediation; within 14 days an unsatisfied complainant may file with the Gaming Commission, which decides within 30 days; appeal to Yurok Tribal Court within 30 days of the Commission decision, with jurisdiction whether or not the individual is a member, and the Tribal Court decision is final.
